meaning_en: Being wise after the event, when it is too late.
conversation:
Rakesh: The office has finally put CCTV cameras everywhere.
Mohona: Three laptops were stolen last month. Now they're careful. Chor palale buddhi bare.
correct: The office took precautions only after the theft had already happened.
literal: Once the thief runs away, people's wits grow sharper.
plausible: The office has always been quick to protect its equipment.

proverb_bn: পড়েছি মোগলের হাতে, খানা খেতে হবে সাথে
romanised: Porechhi Mogoler hate, khana khete hobe sathe.
meaning_en: When you are in someone's power, you have to go along with them.
conversation:
Sourav: You're up at five doing yoga? You never open your eyes before nine.
Bappa: The new hostel warden has made it compulsory, and he can throw us out. Porechhi Mogoler hate, khana khete hobe sathe.
correct: Bappa does the yoga only because the warden has power over him.
literal: A prisoner of the Mughals must sit down and eat every meal with them.
plausible: Bappa has decided on his own to become an early riser.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Mitali: Did you see the comment that man posted under your painting? He says it's the worst thing he's ever seen.
Shyamal: The same man also posted that the earth is flat. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Shyamal won't take the man's insult seriously because the man talks nonsense.
literal: Mad people will say all sorts of things, and goats will eat all sorts of things.
plausible: Shyamal is hurt by the comment and is thinking of giving up painting.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Anjali: Boro-pishi told everyone at the wedding that our new bou is unlucky because it rained.
Ritwik: Boro-pishi says something like that at every wedding. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Ritwik thinks Boro-pishi's remark is silly talk that nobody should take to heart.
literal: There is nothing at all that a madman won't say, and nothing that a goat won't chew.
plausible: Ritwik agrees that the rain on the wedding day really was a bad sign.

proverb_bn: পাগলে কী না বলে, ছাগলে কী না খায়
romanised: Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
meaning_en: Don't take the nonsense of foolish people seriously.
conversation:
Rafiq: The man in the next flat is telling the whole building that I'm a spy because I work at night.
Nadia: He also says his cat talks to him. Pagole ki na bole, chhagole ki na khay.
correct: Nadia tells Rafiq not to worry about the neighbour's absurd accusation.
literal: Crazy people say anything at all, just as goats eat anything.
plausible: Nadia thinks Rafiq should stop working at night so as to avoid suspicion.

meaning_en: People become obedient only when forced.
conversation:
Sumi: My passport file was stuck for months, but it moved in two days once the newspaper ran a story.
Alamgir: Thelar nam babaji.
correct: The office only worked on the file once public pressure pushed it.
literal: 'Respected father' is the polite name given to a hard push.
plausible: The file was delayed only by an ordinary backlog that has now cleared.

proverb_bn: দাঁত থাকতে দাঁতের মর্যাদা বোঝে না
romanised: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
meaning_en: We don't value what we have until we lose it.
conversation:
Arif: I left my old job because the manager was strict, but at least he trained us properly. My new boss doesn't care at all.
Moushumi: Dant thakte danter morjada bojhe na.
correct: Arif didn't appreciate his old manager until he no longer had him.
literal: Teeth are not valued while they are still there in the mouth.
plausible: Moushumi thinks Arif's new boss will turn out to be better in the end.

proverb_bn: কাজের বেলায় কাজি, কাজ ফুরোলে পাজি
romanised: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
meaning_en: People value you only while they need you.
conversation:
Mithu: The Ghoshes called Lokkhi-di every day during their daughter's wedding, and now they've let her go without paying her.
Ma: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
correct: The Ghoshes valued Lokkhi-di only while they needed her help.
literal: During work you are a judge; after the work you are a scoundrel.
plausible: Ma thinks Lokkhi-di didn't do her work properly.

proverb_bn: কাজের বেলায় কাজি, কাজ ফুরোলে পাজি
romanised: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
meaning_en: People value you only while they need you.
conversation:
Joba: During the campaign the candidate visited our slum every evening. Since he won, he won't even take our calls.
Bimal: Kajer belay kaji, kaj phurole paji.
correct: The candidate cared about them only while he needed their votes.
literal: A person is a judge while there is work and a rogue once it's over.
plausible: The candidate is too busy with good work to answer calls.

meaning_en: Becoming lazy or helpless as soon as help is available.
conversation:
Mou: Bubai used to walk to school every day, but since Baba bought the scooter he says his leg hurts and he needs a lift.
Didi: Ghora dekhle khonra.
correct: Bubai has become lazy now that an easier option is available.
literal: Someone suddenly starts to limp as soon as he catches sight of a horse.
plausible: Bubai has genuinely hurt his leg and really needs the lift.

proverb_bn: যারে দেখতে নারি, তার চলন বাঁকা
romanised: Jare dekhte nari, tar cholon banka.
meaning_en: Everything a disliked person does looks wrong.
conversation:
Mukta: If our new neighbours plant flowers, Mrs Rahman says they're showing off; if they keep quiet, she calls them rude.
Habib: Jare dekhte nari, tar cholon banka.
correct: Mrs Rahman dislikes the new neighbours, so she finds fault in everything they do.
literal: The one I can't bear to look at walks crookedly down the road.
plausible: Habib thinks the new neighbours really are rude and showing off.

meaning_en: Going off on an irrelevant tangent.
conversation:
Farhana: The viva was on my thesis, and the external examiner kept asking about my school days in Sylhet.
Rakib: Examiners do that sometimes. Dhan bhante Shiber git.
correct: The examiner wandered into topics unrelated to the thesis.
literal: The examiner was singing a song to Shiva while he husked the rice paddy.
plausible: Rakib thinks the school questions were part of the formal viva.

meaning_en: Speaking beyond one's position or experience.
conversation:
Partha: The intern told the CEO in the meeting that the whole business model is wrong.
Sharmila: Chhoto mukhe boro kotha. He's been here two weeks.
correct: The intern spoke far beyond his position and experience.
literal: Big, grand words came out of the intern's very small mouth.
plausible: Sharmila thinks the intern made a brave and valuable point to the CEO.

meaning_en: Speaking beyond one's position or experience.
conversation:
Kunal: A first-year student stood up at the seminar and corrected the Nobel laureate's economics.
Afsana: Chhoto mukhe boro kotha.
correct: The student spoke far beyond his standing and experience.
literal: Large, important words came out of the student's very small mouth.
plausible: Afsana thinks the student was right to correct the laureate.

meaning_en: The ill wishes of bad people don't harm the good.
conversation:
Moni: Your ex-partner keeps telling everyone your new bakery will shut down within a month.
Ruchira: Let him talk. Shokuner shape goru more na.
correct: Spiteful wishes from a bad person won't harm Ruchira's bakery.
literal: A cow doesn't die just because a vulture has put a curse on it.
plausible: Ruchira is worried the bakery really might close soon.

meaning_en: Everyone knows what is in their own interest.
conversation:
Supriyo: My uncle, who forgets everyone's name, never forgets the date his pension is credited.
Madhuri: Apon bhalo pagoleo bojhe.
correct: Everyone keeps track of what serves their own interest.
literal: Even a madman understands what is good for him.
plausible: Madhuri thinks the uncle is only pretending to be forgetful.

proverb_bn: কানে দিয়েছি তুলো, পিঠে বেঁধেছি কুলো
romanised: Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
meaning_en: Being completely shameless and immune to criticism.
conversation:
Swarup: The whole para complains about the loudspeakers at your club's puja, and you've made them even louder?
Bablu: Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
correct: Bablu is completely unbothered by everyone's criticism of him.
literal: Bablu has stuffed cotton in his ears and tied a winnowing fan to his back.
plausible: Bablu is sorry and will turn the loudspeakers down soon.

proverb_bn: কানে দিয়েছি তুলো, পিঠে বেঁধেছি কুলো
romanised: Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
meaning_en: Being completely shameless and immune to criticism.
conversation:
Shamim: Everyone in the family is criticising your brother for skipping Abba's milad, and he just posted beach photos.
Rina: That's my brother. Kane diyechhi tulo, pithe bendhechhi kulo.
correct: Rina's brother is shameless and immune to all criticism.
literal: He has put cotton in his ears and a fan on his back.
plausible: Rina thinks her brother will apologise to the family this week.

meaning_en: Two people or things that are too different can't get along.
conversation:
Debosmita: My father is a die-hard Mohun Bagan fan and my father-in-law is East Bengal to the bone. Every family dinner ends in a fight.
Farhan: Tele jole mish khay na.
correct: The two fathers are far too different ever to get along.
literal: Oil and water simply cannot mix, however long you stir them together.
plausible: Farhan thinks the two fathers secretly enjoy their dinner fights.

meaning_en: A bad person always finds an excuse.
conversation:
Sohom: The contractor took the advance and vanished. Now it's the cement shortage, then his mother's illness, then the rain.
Jayita: Durjoner chholer obhab hoy na.
correct: A dishonest man like the contractor always finds an excuse.
literal: The contractor literally keeps a supply of excuses stored away.
plausible: Jayita believes the contractor's mother really is seriously ill this time.

proverb_bn: যার কেউ নেই তার ভগবান আছে
romanised: Jar keu nei tar Bhogoban achhe.
meaning_en: God looks after the helpless.
conversation:
Trisha: The stray dog we found injured on the highway was adopted by a vet the very same day.
Mahin: Jar keu nei tar Bhogoban achhe.
correct: A helpless creature with no one gets looked after by heaven.
literal: The stray dog has God living with him on the highway.
plausible: Mahin thinks the vet adopted the dog just to post about it online.

meaning_en: No one can harm a person whom God protects.
conversation:
Pallab: Thakuma's boat sank in the Padma during the storm, and the current carried her to the bank alive.
Anjana: Rakhe Hori mare ke?
correct: Thakuma survived because God protected her, and nothing could harm her.
literal: Someone named Hari kept a firm hold of Thakuma in the river.
plausible: Anjana thinks Thakuma is simply an excellent and strong swimmer.

meaning_en: A self-appointed leader whom no one recognises.
conversation:
Debjit: Nobody elected Mukherjee-babu, but he calls himself the secretary of our building and gives everyone orders.
Sudakshina: Gaye mane na apni morol.
correct: Mukherjee-babu is a self-appointed leader whom nobody recognises.
literal: The village doesn't accept him, but he has made himself the village headman.
plausible: Sudakshina thinks the residents chose Mukherjee-babu as secretary.

proverb_bn: তুমি যাও বঙ্গে, কপাল যায় সঙ্গে
romanised: Tumi jao Bonge, kopal jay shonge.
meaning_en: You can't escape your fate by going somewhere else.
conversation:
Tista: I changed schools to get away from the bullies, and on day one I met a new set of them.
Fardin: Tumi jao Bonge, kopal jay shonge.
correct: Tista's bad luck has followed her right into the new school.
literal: Wherever you go in Bengal, your forehead comes with you.
plausible: Fardin thinks Tista should simply have stayed at her old school.

meaning_en: Fortunate people get things done without effort.
conversation:
Sandipan: Ronny never studies, and the exam got cancelled the day before because of a strike. Now everyone gets average marks.
Kakoli: Bhaggobaner bojha Bhogobane boy.
correct: Things just work out for fortunate people like Ronny without any effort.
literal: God himself is carrying the heavy bundle that Ronny has to carry.
plausible: Kakoli thinks Ronny secretly studied hard for the exam.

meaning_en: Fortunate people get things done without effort.
conversation:
Haripada: My neighbour's land was about to be auctioned for his debts, and then the government said it will buy it for the new highway at double the price.
Shyamoli: Bhaggobaner bojha Bhogobane boy.
correct: Fortune solved the neighbour's problem without him lifting a finger.
literal: God himself takes up the heavy load that the lucky neighbour has to carry.
plausible: Shyamoli thinks the neighbour bribed someone for the highway deal.

meaning_en: Solving a problem without any loss to yourself.
conversation:
Mahbub: The chairman settled the land dispute by giving each brother a share of the government plot. Both are happy, and he lost nothing.
Pakhi: Shapo more lathio na bhange.
correct: The chairman resolved the dispute without losing anything himself.
literal: The snake is dead, and the stick has not been broken.
plausible: Pakhi thinks the chairman gave away too much of the government plot.

meaning_en: If you are good to others, others are good to you.
conversation:
Ashraf: My new boss was strict with everyone, but after I helped her with the move, she's been kind to me every day.
Tahera: Apni bhalo to jogot bhalo.
correct: Ashraf was kind to his boss, so she has been kind to him in return.
literal: If you are fine yourself, then the whole world is also fine.
plausible: Tahera thinks the boss is only being kind to get a favour.

meaning_en: Wrongdoing always catches up with the wrongdoer.
conversation:
Ahana: The influencer who mocked poor people online is now trending for unpaid wages to her own staff.
Tarique: Pap bapkeo chhare na.
correct: The influencer's wrongdoing has caught up with her, as it always does.
literal: Sin does not spare even the influencer's own father at all.
plausible: Tarique thinks the staff are lying to get money from her.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Kibria: Why do you keep praising the union leader on Facebook? You hate him.
Rajon: He decides who gets the overtime. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Rajon praises the leader only because he is forced to.
literal: He calls him father not out of love but because of the jabs.
plausible: Rajon has truly come to like the union leader after all this time.

proverb_bn: সাধে কি বাবা বলি, গুঁতোর চোটে বাবা বলি
romanised: Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
meaning_en: Showing respect only because one is forced to.
conversation:
Moyukh: The new director makes us all clap after his boring speeches, and you clap the loudest.
Faria: My appraisal is next month. Shadhe ki baba boli, gunttor chote baba boli.
correct: Faria shows the director respect only because she is under pressure.
literal: She calls him father only because of the jabs, not from love.
plausible: Faria truly enjoys the director's speeches more than anyone.

meaning_en: When you need something, you have to do things you'd rather not.
conversation:
Arkadeep: Riju hates his cousin, but he's been calling him every day since he found out the cousin works at the passport office.
Pampa: Goroj boro balai.
correct: Riju puts up with his cousin because he wants a favour.
literal: Need is a terrible plague that has come down on Riju's household.
plausible: Pampa thinks Riju and his cousin have finally made up.

meaning_en: When you need something, you have to do things you'd rather not.
conversation:
Hafiz: Rezaul swore he'd never set foot in his in-laws' house, but he's there every weekend now that his business needs his father-in-law's loan.
Dolly: Goroj boro balai.
correct: Rezaul is swallowing his pride because he wants the loan badly.
literal: Need is a dreadful curse that has fallen on Rezaul.
plausible: Dolly thinks Rezaul has truly made peace with his in-laws at last.

meaning_en: Unequal treatment for people in the same situation.
conversation:
Parijat: Both of us were late by the same ten minutes, but only I got a warning letter. Rohit got a smile.
Swagatika: Ek jatray prithok phol.
correct: Parijat was punished while Rohit, just as late, was not.
literal: Two people on the same journey ended up with different results.
plausible: Swagatika thinks Rohit had a good excuse for coming late.

proverb_bn: পরের জন্য গর্ত খুঁড়লে নিজেকেই সে গর্তে পড়তে হয়
romanised: Porer jonno gorto khunrle nijekei she gorte porte hoy.
meaning_en: Harm planned for others comes back on you.
conversation:
Ahona: Kushal spread rumours that his colleague was stealing, and the investigation found that he was the one fiddling the accounts.
Ratul: Porer jonno gorto khunrle nijekei she gorte porte hoy.
correct: Kushal's plan to harm his colleague came back on him instead.
literal: Whoever digs a pit for someone else ends up tumbling into that pit himself.
plausible: Ratul thinks the colleague framed Kushal in the investigation.

meaning_en: Using what you learned from someone against them.
conversation:
Nirjhar: Sen-babu trained Raju in the sweet-making business for ten years, and now Raju has opened a shop right next door and stolen his customers.
Gitali: Guru mara bidya.
correct: Raju is using what Sen-babu taught him to defeat Sen-babu himself.
literal: Raju learned a skill that is used for killing one's teacher.
plausible: Gitali thinks Sen-babu is happy to see Raju doing so well.
